The challenge for Canada, as 1 see it, and for the Canadian economy, has always been to increase the manufacturing or processing of goods in Canada, to create jobs in Canada and to reduce the exports of unprocessed raw materials Canadians, going back a century, have always tried to diversify our economy. We face the same challenge today. Our resource sector is declining and there is an inevitable move away from resources. There are a number of reasons for this. First, developing countries have increased the supply of resources such as coal, pulpwood, copper, nickel and iron ore. Second, this new supply of resources from developing countries has coincided with the slowdown in global growth. Third, there has been increased competition from what are known as new industrial materials. Copper is being replaced by fibre optics, and steel is being replaced by plastics and light metals such aluminium. The average man on the street knows that tennis rackets today are made out of graphite. The Macdonald Commission published figures which demonstrated that between 1964 and 1984 Canadian exports of food, mainly wheat, and crude and fabricated materials, dropped from 84 per cent of Canada's exports to 56 per cent.
Recently, the chairman of the Department of Food Sciences of a university in Western Canada asked me: "By the year 2000, will Canada export any wheat?" He provided his own answer. He said: "I doubt it". I would refer Hon. Members to an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail on September 20 which asks a rather startling question: "Should Canada quit farming?" I am not from western Canada but we have a lot of agriculture in Quebec. I am from an urban area, but I am sure that Hon. Members from rural areas would admit that this is a rather provocative and startling question. The article begins by saying:
Canada prides itself on being the bread-basket of the world, but the reality is something else.
Rank Canadian farmers with their international brethren, and they fall into place well down the line. France grows more wheat than Canada, and the value of farm products from both California and Iowa is greater than that for all of Canada. Even China and India, using little more than hand labour and Iron Age tools, outclass Canada when it comes to growing wheat.
I do not think I have to remind Hon. Members that the Government last month offered farmers nearly $50 million to go out of business. Anyone who has followed the trade talks- although the talks are being conducted behind closed doors-I think would agree that if there is any conclusion that can be drawn from those talks to date it is that it is going to be tougher to export our national resources and agricultural products. We are seeing, with the dispute over the export of cedar shakes and shingles, that either through voluntary

October 7, 1986
The Address-Mr. Berger
restraint or through increased stumpage or increased duties, the United States wants us to reduce our exports of lumber products. The only solution for Canada, the only way to maintain the high standard of living we have been accustomed to, is to use our knowledge and skills to better develop new products than the competition. This does not mean to say that we abandon our resource of our agricultural sectors, nor our textiles and clothing. On the contrary. We can build on our strength in these areas to develop new products.
This is not just theory. I recently spent a week or 10 days visiting a number of firms which have participated in the National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program, the program I referred to in my question to the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie). I visited a Toronto research company which has helped a number of firms in the agricultural and food industries use technology to develop new products for both domestic and international markets. For example, there is a company in the egg processing industry in Winnipeg which breaks one-half million eggs a day. It has developed a technology which removes water from the eggs and it exports powdered egg whites to Japan. The company also extracts an enzyme from the eggs which is also exported to Japan. That particular company is the largest producer of this enzyme in the world.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I also visited some plants in Saint-Valerien and Drummondville where new equipment has been developed for the lumber industry, not to mention snow blowers to be used on highways and on airport runways. 1 visited a company in Quebec City which has improved on existing products and has developed new ones thanks again to that industrial research program. The company is building industrial washers for hospitals and restaurants. In Montreal, I visited a company which has developed a new product to test jet motors for the Pratt & Whitney Company, a minimum investment by the Government of some $70,000 which has allowed the company to make sales worth $1.5 million this year.
I trust that these few examples demonstrate that we can build on our strength to diversify our economy. However, what is the record of the Conservative Government in research and development? First, I suggest that one has to go back to the promises made prior to the last election campaign and during that election campaign. We all remember the Prime Minister's best selling book-among Conservatives-entitled Where I Stand. The Prime Minister wrote the following in 1983:
The starting line for me is the technological dimension. Either we go into the game and become important players in this major league or we become a nation that will, during its entire lifetime, play in the Junior B circuit.
Research and development, and the resulting innovations, are the lifeblood of a successful economy and country.
He also urged that Canada's research and development efforts be exempted from government restraint programs.
Instead, he called for a doubling of research and development spending by both the public and private sectors.
Since the election, rather than increased spending on R and D, as promised, we have seen cuts in almost all areas of government scientific support. The Science Council had its $5 million budget cut by one-half. In 1984, the National Research Council had $70 million cut from its budget of $500 million. The granting councils which provide funds for university research and research training had their budgets frozen. In June, we learned that the National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program, to which I have been referring, was cut by $60 million over five years. This represents close to 20 per cent of its budget. As a consequence of these cuts Canada's research and development effort fell in the first part of 1986, for the first time in 15 years, with the exception of 1983.

The scientific community is frustrated and disappointed. They had put so much hope in this Government. It is possible, Mr. Speaker, that those who support increased expenditures for research and development have failed to convince decisionmakers that research is of the utmost importance for the economic future of the country. It is also possible, Mr. Speaker, that the average Canadian finds it difficult to see any relation between research and his own job. The same could be said of the Prime Minister. He does not see any relation between his election commitments and the preservation of his own job. Well, I will try today to explain that relation.
During my visits, 1 met with many businessmen and I will tell you now about some of their comments. 1 particularly remember a conversation with a businessman from Quebec City, a founding member of the Groupement quebecois d'entreprises. This organization is made up of some 500 small-and medium-sized businesses whose turnover varies between $2.5 and $3 million and which have an average staff of 50 employees. During the last five years the group has made a substantial effort to increase its members' awareness of the importance of research and development.
I am told that initially, members of the group thought research was something for big companies. It was necessary to explain to members that for them, development was more likely to mean adapting existing technology to their products or their manufacturing processes.
I was also told, Mr. Speaker, that the typical entrepreneur is the guy who has a patent on his invention. It may not be perfect, it may not be high technology, but it is new, and the main thing is that it makes a profit. Often, however, the entrepreneur meets with obstacles. He has to deal with a problem in terms of product quality or the manufacturing process. For instance, he may have a welding problem, but the typical entrepreneur doesn't know about material resistance. He doesn't know about welding and he doesn't know how to solve his problem. He doesn't have the technical know-how.
October 7, 1986

Mr. Speaker, that is where the IRAP program comes in. The program makes it possible for entrepreneurs to consult experts, post-graduate students who come to the company to work on a specific problem for three or four months, to try and find the answer. Someone told me that IRAP is a small program that gives experts a chance to focus on a particular detail.
Mr. Speaker, the results are incredible. Companies that were not moving four or five years ago have developed new products which today are responsible for the majority of their sales. Often, experts or academics hired for this three-or four-month period have become research directors for the same companies. Today, they are leading a research team of four or five or more. That same Quebec businessman also said that IRAP and another program sponsored by the Government of Quebec have helped the entrepreneur to approach academics. At first, the entrepreneur thinks that the university is going to upset his business and he is afraid of the academic. It is necessary to overcome this mistrust and the entrepreneur must be encouraged to work on development. IRAP has often been successfully in doing so.
From the information I have seen, a number of companies would not be in existence today without research and the program sponsored by IRAP. Most new products did not exist four or five years ago.
Another point, all company directors I met were asked the following question: "Would you have done this research without the support of IRAP?" And the answer was unanimous: No. Why? Well, because these small businesses often lack the financial resources, and besides, the program gave them the kind of credibility that allowed them to seek financing elsewhere.
Mr. Speaker, it is against this background that we should evaluate the new promises made in the Speech from the Throne. I must say it is encouraging to see the priority given to research, on paper. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, again I can give some graphic examples of young people with masters degrees and doctoral degrees who have found employment in the private sector in the past few years thanks to the Industrial Research and Assistance Program. Mr. Speaker, over the past summer I spent most of my time talking with my constituents. Of course 1 talked with them in my office, on their own doorsteps, and at various community meetings. As Your Honour can imagine, there was a variety of subjects which were concerning them over the course of the summer. 1 am sure you will not find it a surprise that they talked with me about the Post Office, the question of capital punishment, the Tamil refugees, and even about building penitentiaries in the riding of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Despite all those things, if there was one over-all recurring problem about which they spoke with me most, it was the whole question of gasoline prices. My constituents understand, as do all other Canadians, that the price of a barrel of oil has fallen very substantially over the past few months. Of course they understand that that is creating hardships for Canadians in the oil producing parts of the country. As well they understand that they probably must share some of the burden in order to help Canadians, who are suffering as a result, over the hurdle. They understand all that, but they do not understand, with the price of a barrel of oil falling and with the fact that other Canadians are out of work because of falling oil prices, why that is not reflected more in the price they pay for gasoline at the pumps.
Particularly they do not understand why there is such a difference between the price of gasoline in the United States and here in Canada. They do not understand why when they go to the United States they pay something like 69 cents American per gallon, or in Canadian terms 20 cents Canadian per litre, and when they return to Toronto they pay something like 36 cents Canadian per litre, or if they come here to Ottawa they pay more like 41 cents Canadian per litre.
I tried to explain to them that the difference probably was reflected mainly in taxes, taxes which provincial and federal Governments imposed in order to improve our lot in life and to improve our wonderful social security system which of course
October 7, 1986

Americans do not have. That very well may be the case, they say, but why is it that there is such a wide spread in prices between leaded and unleaded gasoline in Canada as opposed to the United States? They pointed out to me that in Canada the price spread between leaded and unleaded gasoline is something like three cents to four cents Canadian per litre, while in the United States it is something like two cents American per gallon or, in Canadian terms, one-half cent Canadian per litre. This means that the price spread is something like 5.5 times greater in Canada than it is in the United States, notwithstanding the fact that the Parliamentary Secretary is shaking his head.
At the same time they pointed out to me that in a recent article in The Financial Post, Imperial Oil or Esso indicated that it only costs one-half cent Canadian per litre more to produce unleaded gasoline than it does to produce leaded gasoline.
1 answered them by saying that it was the taxes and the social security system which we have in Canada. They came right back at me and said: "Okay, but why is it that in West Germany unleaded gasoline costs two cents per litre less than leaded gasoline, even though it costs more to produce unleaded gasoline than it does to produce leaded gasoline?" The fact is, they say, that the taxes in West Germany make a heck of a lot more sense than the taxes on gasoline in this country. In fact this country is encouraging people to buy leaded gas instead of unleaded gas. Of course that is creating more acid rain and more pollution. I did not have a wonderful answer to that, so I came back to Ottawa and in our first Question Period I asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse) that question. After I heard his answer, I was just as confused as my constituents.
I am here today to ask the Parliamentary Secretary whether he can give me a better explanation so that I will feel more at ease and my constituents will not feel that they are being ripped off.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) who always represents his constituents very well here in the House of Commons. His concern for consumers is legend. I appreciate him drawing this matter to the attention of the House of Commons.
I think the Hon. Member will find that since there has been a dramatic drop in the price of a barrel of oil that the corresponding drop in the price of a litre of gasoline has corresponded to that drop. Also, this summer we experienced gas wars in our particular area of Ontario. These wars are going on in the West at the present and this has to do with marketing. Generally speaking, the price of a litre of gasoline has dropped from 52 cents a litre for regular leaded gasoline to 35 cents to 41 cents a litre for regular leaded gasoline, depending on the market.
Adjournment Debate
First, I want to emphasize that the Government does not set gasoline prices. They are dictated by the market-place. We are seeing that in this country with the various markets and the competition that we have. I just mentioned the prices which vary from day to day and week to week. It is very confusing when the consumer sees prices going up and down. But that is the market-place at work. It is the same as your shirt, your suit or a tie being on sale. Competition is at work in the marketplace. It is healthy and it helps the consumer.
Yes, there is a price differential in a litre of gas comparable to a litre of gas in the U.S. Forty per cent is made up of taxes and the other 60 per cent is market differential. There is no question about that and that explains the price differential.
With regard to the Member's question, namely the difference between leaded and unleaded gasoline prices, I am going to use figures for July because they are the latest average figures we have for both Canada and the United States on a comparable basis. The average price differential in July between leaded and unleaded gasoline was approximately 1.9 cents per litre higher in Canada than in the United States. At that time the average Canadian price of gasoline, in Canadian cents per litre so we do not have to do any conversions, was 41.5 cents for regular leaded-this is all Canada average-and 45.4 cents for regular unleaded, a 3.9 cent a litre differential. The corresponding prices in the United States were 29.8 cents and 31.8 cents a litre, a 2 cent a litre differential. Those are the facts, not the figures mentioned by the Member earlier.
It is interesting to note that the Canadian average is influenced by the higher unleaded gasoline volumes sold in Quebec where the leaded/unleaded differential is the largest in the country, which throws the average out quite a bit. Of the differential, four-tenths of 1 cent is accredited to taxes. The rest is the higher octane component which is more expensive to put into the gasoline. The Hon. Member mentioned a figure of one of the oil companies. I cannot substantiate that. Notwithstanding these products-costs differences, it is the market, not the Government, which ultimately sets the prices of both grades.

subtopic: PHARMACEUTICAL PRODUCTS A) RECOMMENDATION OF THE EASTMAN COMMISSION-GOVERNMENT POSITION B) PRICE OF NEW DRUGS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
PHARMACEUTICAL PRODUCTS A) RECOMMENDATION OF THE EASTMAN COMMISSION-GOVERNMENT POSITION B) PRICE OF NEW DRUGS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I take the floor this evening it is because the answer of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) to my question concerning drug patents is vague, incomplete and open to interpretation.
When I raised the matter 1 wanted to know whether the Minister was considering the possibility of bringing his Bill in line with the recommendations contained in the Eastman Commission report.

October 7, 1986
Adjournment Debate
The Minister said no. But, Mr. Speaker, the Minister is right to suggest that it was the Liberal Party which raised the possibility of amending the drug patents legislation. That is why we appointed the Eastman Commission. To us in the Liberal Party, the recommendations contained in the commission report seemed reasonable, and for several reasons. First, it was an independent inquiry and, as such, less subject to possible pressures from various interest groups. Second, the commission made recommendations which took into consideration the needs of all those involved in this industry, including consumers, innovating companies, generic companies, the scientific community as well as the provinces.
The Minister replied that he had considered the pros and cons of his solution. He came to the conclusion that the advantages of the proposition made last June are more numerous and significant than the existing advantage, which is control over declining drug prices.
So, Mr. Speaker, I find it necessary to go back in time and remind the Minister that price control is not the main purpose of the 1969 amendments. High drug prices in Canada before 1969 were nothing more than a symptom of an overly concentrated drug industry. This fact was amply demonstrated in three reports published before 1969. I will merely mention the report of the House of Commons Restrictrive Trade Practices Committee and the Harley report. Both reports dealt with the manufacturing and marketing of pharmaceuticals. They showed that the drug industry has made excessive profits and has imposed unreasonable costs to Canadian consumers.
What we have here is an industry which before 1969 had no hesitation making huge profits on the backs of Canadians. That industry asked the Government for changes, and those changes were studied by an independent committee. The latter recommended that steps be taken to maintain a balance between the various interests involved. Despite all those democratic efforts, the Minister has succeeded in giving all of the pie to the drug industry, claiming that the benefits of that policy are better than the recommendations of an independent committee.
As you will agree, Mr. Speaker, this is quite amazing.
The 1969 amendments were aimed at fostering greater competition in a monopolistic industry. There is every indication that we succeeded. We developed a situation where we have lower prices, greater choice in drug prices, and, above all, we set up the makings of a Canadian pharmaceutical industry, in the form of generic drug companies, without endangering the profitability of the general drug industry in the opinion of the Eastman Committee.
Today the Minister answered that the benefits of such drastic changes are better than the current situation, better than the Eastman report recommendations. The burden of proof rests on his shoulders. The Minister went further when addressing my second question. He would not say whether the prices of new drugs would be higher. He said: higher compared with what? Compared with prices paid now, Mr. Speaker.
More specifically, compared with those paid between 1969 and 1986. The Minister seems to rely on the good will of innovative companies. Also he seems to believe that price increases are not likely. He went on saying that he would set up a review board for drug prices. Which means that the Minister expects increases in the prices of drugs; otherwise, he would not have felt necessary to set up a watch-dog organization to monitor prices.
For that matter, during the public hearing held by the Liberal Party on September 23 last, the Consumers' Association of Canada advised us of its experience with price control boards such as the one proposed by the Minister.
In its opinion, price control boards make it possible for corporations to get away with huge profits at the expense of consumers. It is nothing but a legal front to justify high prices. The Consumers' Association of Canada told us that these monitoring boards are outright failures and that it is not much encouraged by the prospect of a new one.
To conclude, I repeat that the burden of proof remains with the Minister. If he should persist in not addressing the issues we are raising in good faith, he will give rise to a great many suspicions concerning these initiatives. The Minister should and must demonstrate the so-called great benefits which Canada would have got from his proposal. He should demand from the companies a copy of all feasibility studies or, better still, any concrete plan which would cause us to say: Yes, the Bill makes sense. In fact, we would appreciate any study in this area by the innovating companies, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and of course the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. You will understand that I am acting and speaking as an ordinary citizen when I ask you to show and explain the basis for your decision, Mr. Minister. The people are very wary of Governments these days. We must all do our share to try and improve this image. 1 hope the Minister is prepared to do his share, since otherwise, the Government's proposal will look like a conspiracy against the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, in response to the question raised, we will first be proposing measures to exploit the significant potential of the pharmaceutical sector, turning it into what we would consider to be a world-class, highly innovative industry characterized by strong growth in investment, employment, research and development and manufacturing activity. Second, and perhaps equally as important, we propose to ensure that Canadians will continue to benefit from reasonable drug prices.
These are our objectives. To reach them, the Government has built upon the recommendations of the Eastman Commission which concluded that our patent policy was in need of rebalancing in a manner that will provide strong incentives for new investment and growth in the industry while safeguarding

the interests of consumers. The prices of drugs already on the market will not be affected one bit by our policy proposals. It is also important to keep in mind that the benefit of generic drug competition will continue.
Remember that currently only 7 per cent of prescription drug sales are subject to generic competition. Canadians have no way of knowing if they are paying a fair price for the remaining 93 per cent of drugs on pharmacy shelves. The Drug Prices Review Board will have a mandate to review all prescription drug prices. The Board will be assessing drug prices in relation to factors such as the Consumer Price Index, the actual production costs of the drug and the price of similar drugs in other countries.
I would also like to draw Members' attention to a major provision of the proposed policy which requires a thorough review of this policy after a four-year period. If it is evident that the policy is not working or that the industry has not met its commitments, the Government will change the policy.
The innovative sector of the industry has made a firm commitment to increase its ratio of R and D to sales to a level of 8 per cent by 1990 and 10 per cent by 1995, which is double the existing level of less than 5 per cent. These undertakings translate into an additional investment in R and D activity of $1.4 billion over the next 10 years. In 1995, R and D outlays will exceed $600 million per year. Some 30 per cent of these expenditures will flow to Canadian universities, hospitals and research establishments.
In the process, we forecast that 3,000 scientific and research-related jobs will be directly created-opportunities that are badly needed for our university graduates. The manufacturing provisions are likely to generate additional new jobs in the chemical manufacturing sector. The added protection afforded pharmaceutical discoveries will not only foster growth in R and D, but should also translate into a greater volume of manufacturing and export activity in the Canadian drug industry. subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-REASONS OF PRIME MINISTER FOR CHOOSING HIS OWN RIDING
PENITENTIARIES-REASONS OF PRIME MINISTER FOR CHOOSING HIS OWN RIDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I wish to congratulate you on your appointment as Deputy Speaker, and 1 am sure you will perform your duties with your customary distinction and style.
Mr. Speaker, today I put a question to the Prime Minister about the Conservative Government's decision to build a new penitentiary at Port-Cartier in the Prime Minister's riding. The Prime Minister tried to justify this decision by implying that the unemployment rate in his riding is very high.
Earlier today, Mr. Speaker, 1 gave some figures on the unemployment rate in many other ridings in the Province of Quebec and I asked the Prime Minister to explain to the
Adjournment Debate
House and to Quebecers why he did not build this penitentiary elsewhere if indeed the real reason was the high unemployment rate in his riding.
For instance, Mr. Speaker, in April 1985 when the Government decided to build the penitentiary in the Prime Minister's riding, the unemployment rate in Port-Cartier was 13 per cent. Much too high, of course, but then the unemployment rate was 22 per cent in Rimouski, 15.6 per cent in Chicoutimi, and 19.6 per cent in Gaspe.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it stands to reason that it was not because the unemployment rate was very high that the penitentiary was to be built in the riding of the Prime Minister. On the contrary, it was simply a gift made to the voters in the Prime Minister's riding. Well, Mr. Speaker, it was a gift which is costing a lot of money to Canadian taxpayers-at least $16 million more in capital expenditures and at least $3 million a year to operate the penitentiary. Not to mention, Mr. Speaker, the question of the remoteness of families and correctional service professionals from this penitentiary in Port-Cartier. This is why all agencies related to correctional services unanimously censure the Conservative Government for making this decision.
Mr. Speaker, it was not a coincidence that the penitentiary is to be located in the Prime Minister's riding, some 400 kilometres from the major urban centre of Quebec City.
1 would note that the announcement of the prison at Port-Cartier was in fact made on June 18, which was over two weeks before Treasury Board approved this decision. That is no coincidence. As every Member of the House knows, the reality is that this was blatant political pork-barrelling by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to look after his own riding. It is one thing if that does not cost any extra money, but as I pointed out, what the Prime Minister is doing is looking after his own constituents on the North Shore of Quebec at the very considerable expense of Canadian taxpayers.
Not only that, he is locating a prison in an isolated area of Quebec in which services are lacking and in which the possibility of family reunification-that important and fundamental link between the families and friends of prisoners-is totally lacking. That has been condemned as well.
The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret)-
[ Translation]
Mr. de Cotret implied that the decision had been made in February 1984. However, Mr. Speaker, the facts do not confirm this. In February 1984 a Liberal Government was in office and it had decided to build the penitentiary in Drum-mondville, not in Port-Cartier. Apparently, the President of the Treasury Board made a mistake to protect the Prime Minister.

October 7, 1986
Adjournment Debate

But Canadians know better. Canadians are asking themselves if it is really necessary to build another maximum security prison in this country at all. Is it really a priority at this time to spend some $70 million to build a new maximum security prison? I suggest that it is rather obscene to have this battle between one region and another as to who is going to have the prison in their particular region. We do not construct prisons in this country as regional economic development projects. We build prisons if there is a demonstrated need and we build them where they are correctionally sound. This particular project falls down on both counts.
The Liberals did the same thing in building a prison in Renous, the Atlantic institution in the Province of New Brunswick. They said they were building it for economic development reasons and, of course, it was political patronage by the Liberals as well. It is time we placed a moratorium on the construction of new prisons in this country. It is certainly time that we re-examine the fundamental philosophy underlying the correctional system. We imprison too many people and in many cases sentences are too long. In this particular case, not only was the construction of the prison wrong, but the abuse of the Prime Minister's Office, for his own personal political gain at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada, is shocking and shameful.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gordon Towers (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-REASONS OF PRIME MINISTER FOR CHOOSING HIS OWN RIDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, and it has been stated in the House at various times over the past few days, this Government is committed to addressing the problem of regional disparity. Upon taking office in September, 1984, our Government ordered a freeze on major capital expenditures in order to determine which projects could best address the problem of regional disparity and to decide which projects should proceed.
The Correctional Services of Canada required additional beds for maximum and protective custody inmates. The Government decided rather than build another penitentiary beside Drummond in Drummondville, that in the interests of
regional development another site in a regionally depressed area should be chosen.
As the Hon. Member knows, parts of northern Quebec suffer from very high rates of unemployment. The Government chose to locate the required facility in Port-Cartier due to its high level of unemployment and to stimulate the local economy. The Government offers no apology for assisting the region.
It is estimated that the institution will directly employ 223 persons and it is expected to create an additional 200 jobs in the area. Many of these new jobs will go to local people and plans are well under way to accommodate this. The Port-Cartier facility will meet the need as identified by the Correctional Services of Canada for protective custody in Quebec. The need was identified and the Government, in the interests of regional development, chose a site where a prison could be built to achieve both CSC's requirement and relieve regional disparity. Just because Canadians happen to live in a Prime Minister's constituency, does the Hon. Member believe they should not be given the same consideration as other people across Canada?
In summary, the reasons for building the institution in Port-Cartier, Quebec, are relatively straightforward. First, there was a need for a protective custody penitentiary in the Province of Quebec; second, as Port-Cartier suffered from a very high rate of unemployment, it was felt that the penitentiary should be built in Port-Cartier to address the problems of regional disparity.
The Government has absolutely no apology to make for the decision to use the construction of a major facility as a measure to relieve regional disparity. That is the reason the Government made the decision and that is why this Government stands firmly behind its decision and its policy to assist depressed areas of our country.
